Cerebellar contributions to action and cognition: Prediction, timescale, and continuity

The cerebellum is the optimizer most naturally described as a system for predictive calibration. If the cortex learns a hierarchical generative model of the world, and the basal ganglia learn which actions, policies, and behavioral programs are worth selecting, the cerebellum learns how to make selected policies run accurately through the physics of a body and the timing constraints of a nervous system. Its canonical domain is movement, but its computational signature is more general: it receives high-dimensional contextual and efference-copy signals, expands them into a very large basis set, uses sparse teaching signals to detect when predicted and actual consequences diverge, and returns precisely timed corrections to downstream motor, autonomic, cognitive, and affective loops 3, 4, 1. In this sense, the cerebellum is not primarily a system for deciding what to do. It is a system for learning the fast internal models that allow an already-selected behavior to be executed smoothly, continuously, and with minimal error. Recent reviews frame the cerebellum’s motor contribution around speed and accuracy, feedforward control, associative learning, and internal model-based prediction rather than simple "coordination" alone 4. An anatomical plate labels cerebellar lobes and neighboring brainstem structures (Figure) 40. A textbook microcircuit diagram shows the major cerebellar cell types and inputs (Figure) 41.

The need for such a system is easiest to see in movement. Motor commands do not act on a simple plant. They act on a many-jointed, nonlinear, noisy, delayed body whose parts mechanically perturb one another. A command to move the shoulder alters the dynamics of the elbow; a rapid reach generates interaction torques; a change in posture changes the mapping from muscle activation to endpoint motion; and sensory feedback arrives too late to be used as a purely reactive controller. A nervous system that waited passively for proprioceptive and visual feedback would always be controlling the body’s past state. The cerebellum appears to solve this problem by learning forward models: internal simulations that use current state, context, and efference copy to predict the sensory consequences of actions before delayed feedback arrives 3, 4, 5. These predictions can be used for state estimation, rapid online correction, cancellation of self-generated sensory input, and anticipatory compensation for the inertial and interaction dynamics of the body 6, 4. The cerebellum therefore occupies a niche complementary to both cortex and basal ganglia: cortex can represent goals, policies, body schemas, and world states; basal ganglia can bias selection among candidate actions; but the cerebellum calibrates the timing and gain structure required for those selected actions to land accurately in the physical world 7, 8.

This division of labor is visible in computational models that combine basal ganglia and cerebellar learning. In one recent systems-level model, the cortex-basal ganglia loop learned to map desired outcomes onto concrete actions, while the cerebellum minimized the remaining aiming error; the authors summarized the distinction by concluding that the cortex-basal ganglia loop learns through a novelty-based motor prediction error to determine concrete actions, whereas the cerebellum reduces the residual error of the selected movement 9. This is, however, not meant to imply a rigid serial pipeline. The basal ganglia, cerebellum, thalamus, brainstem, and cortex form interacting loops, and cerebellar outputs can influence both cortical dynamics and basal-ganglia-related circuits. But it does capture a useful computational asymmetry: the basal ganglia are naturally framed around selection, reinforcement, vigor, exploration, and policy commitment, while the cerebellum is naturally framed around supervised calibration, prediction, timing, and error-based refinement 10, 11, 7.

Evolutionarily, this computational role is plausible because the cerebellum appears to have expanded with exactly the kinds of control problems that make pure feedback inadequate. As bodies become larger, sensorimotor delays become more consequential: a signal from the periphery takes longer to arrive, the limb may have moved substantially by the time feedback is processed, and destabilizing corrections can arrive out of phase with the state they are meant to fix. As motor repertoires expand, the organism must also handle a larger space of limb configurations, self-generated sensory consequences, and interaction torques. A high-capacity predictive controller is therefore increasingly valuable: it can learn mappings from context and motor command to future sensory state, allowing control to be based on an estimate of what the body will be doing rather than what it was doing tens or hundreds of milliseconds ago 4, 6. This does not mean the cerebellum is purely a "millisecond-scale" device. Its most distinctive advantage is temporal precision, especially in the tens-to-hundreds-of-milliseconds range of sensorimotor prediction and conditioned responses, but the same architecture can contribute to longer behavioral sequences, cognitive timing, language, social interaction, and affective regulation when embedded in slower cortical loops 1, 2. Diedrichsen’s 2026 account describes a cerebellar circuit in which Purkinje cells learn to predict climbing-fiber input from high-dimensional parallel-fiber patterns, with predictions often timed tens to hundreds of milliseconds before the teaching event 1.

The symptoms of cerebellar disease illustrate what happens when this predictive calibration fails. Cerebellar lesions do not usually paralyze muscles or abolish the desire to move. Instead they produce dysmetria, decomposition of movement, intention tremor, impaired adaptation, poor timing, instability, and a striking loss of smooth coordination. These are the symptoms expected from an engineered control system that has lost its forward model: the controller still issues commands, but it no longer accurately compensates for delay, noise, inertia, multi-joint coupling, or the changing gain of the body across contexts 12, 4, 13. In reaching, speech, posture, eye movements, and locomotion, the deficit is not merely weakness but miscalibration: errors are detected too late, corrections are over- or under-scaled, and movement breaks into a sequence of late feedback corrections rather than unfolding as a continuous feedforward trajectory 14, 15. Recent work on corrective submovements further sharpens this view by linking reactive corrections to the training of future anticipatory cerebellar control signals 14.

The same computational motif appears to extend beyond overt movement. Human neuroimaging and anatomical work show that large portions of the cerebellum are coupled not to primary motor cortex but to association networks, including prefrontal, parietal, temporal, default-mode, language, executive-control, salience, social-cognitive, and affective systems 16, 17, 18. Buckner and colleagues’ intrinsic-connectivity work was perhaps especially important, showing that much of the human cerebellum is functionally coupled to cerebral association cortex rather than motor cortex alone 16. Subsequent task-based and multi-dataset atlases have refined this picture, identifying cerebellar territories associated with sensorimotor control, attention, executive control, language, mentalizing/default-mode function, and small limbic territories 17, 18. A 2026 preprint examines nonmotor cerebellar learning in humans (Figure) 42. The preprint compares candidate computational models (Figure).

This non-motor expansion does not require abandoning the forward-model view. It suggests instead that cerebellar modules may learn predictive models for any domain in which temporally structured internal dynamics must be calibrated against delayed consequences. In language, the cerebellum may help predict the timing, sequencing, and sensory consequences of speech and comprehension; in social cognition, it may help anticipate the unfolding of another agent’s behavior; in affect, it may help regulate the timing and gain of autonomic and emotional responses; and in cognition, it may help coordinate distributed cortical communication by shaping thalamo-cortical dynamics 1, 19, 20, 21, 22. The cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome supports this broader view clinically: lesions can impair executive function, visuospatial cognition, language, and affective regulation even when the primary deficit is not a simple motor impairment 23, 24. A recent PLOS Biology review emphasizes that many cerebellar regions form loops with non-motor cortical areas and that cerebellar activation is reliable across cognitive tasks, while also warning that the precise cognitive teaching signals carried by climbing fibers remain unresolved 1.

The reward literature further complicates, but also enriches, the simple “supervised motor error” picture. Classical cerebellar theories emphasized climbing fibers as motor-error teaching signals that train parallel-fiber-to-Purkinje synapses 25, 26, 27. Yet recent work shows reward-related signals in granule cells, Purkinje-cell complex spikes and simple spikes, molecular-layer interneurons, and cerebellar nuclei, as well as anatomical interactions between cerebellum, basal ganglia, ventral tegmental area, and prefrontal cortex 28. This does not make the cerebellum “just another reinforcement-learning system.” Rather, it suggests that the teaching signals available to cerebellar modules can be task-specific: motor errors in motor loops, sensory surprise in perceptual loops, reward or outcome signals in reward-associated loops, and possibly abstract prediction failures in cognitive loops 28, 1. The safest generalization is therefore not that the cerebellum always learns motor errors, but that it learns precisely timed predictive mappings from high-dimensional context to future teaching-signal events. A 2024 consensus paper explicitly describes the cerebellum as building internal models, predicting how actions affect state, updating those models when predicted and actual outcomes mismatch, and participating in reward mechanisms alongside basal ganglia and prefrontal systems 28.

Anatomically, the cerebellum is unusually well matched to this algorithm, and each of its components will reappear in the subsections that follow. Its inputs arrive through two excitatory systems that map naturally onto the two halves of a predict–compare loop. Mossy fibers, arising from pontine, spinal, vestibular, reticular, and other precerebellar nuclei, carry contextual, sensory, motor, and cortical information into the granule-cell layer and send collaterals to the deep cerebellar nuclei. They supply the context from which predictions are made. Climbing fibers, arising from the inferior olive, deliver powerful but sparse teaching signals to Purkinje cells and also send collaterals to the nuclei 29, 4, 1. The output of the cerebellar cortex runs through a single cell type: Purkinje cells, which are inhibitory and project to the deep cerebellar and vestibular nuclei. These nuclei in turn send cerebellar output to motor, premotor, prefrontal, parietal, brainstem, vestibular, red-nucleus, and thalamic targets 29, 30, 31. The basic loop is therefore cortico-ponto-cerebellar input, transformation in the cerebellar cortex, integration in the nuclei, and output through cerebello-thalamo-cortical or cerebello-brainstem pathways. These loops are topographically organized, so different cerebellar territories are linked to different body parts and cortical networks 16, 32. This anatomy sets up the rest of the section. "Cerebellar Loss Functions" asks what the mossy-fiber context is used to predict. "Cerebellar Error Signals" follows the two input streams in detail: how granule cells recode mossy-fiber input into the Purkinje simple-spike prediction, where the climbing-fiber error is actually computed, and how the olive keeps that error so precisely timed. "Cerebellar Plasticity" turns to how the climbing-fiber signal rewrites parallel-fiber synapses onto Purkinje cells and how the mossy-fiber collaterals allow learning in the nuclei themselves. Finally, "Cerebellar Learning in Action" shows the whole loop at work in vestibulo-ocular reflex adaptation, eyeblink conditioning, reaching, and speech. A recent bilateral connectome makes this circuit architecture explicit (Figure) 39. A recent bilateral connectome makes this circuit architecture explicit (Figure).

Internally, the cerebellar cortex is resembles a repeated engineered module. Across lobules and functional territories, the same microcircuit is reused: mossy fibers excite granule cells; granule cells send parallel fibers across Purkinje-cell dendritic arbors; Purkinje cells inhibit nuclear neurons; climbing fibers deliver powerful complex-spike events; and inhibitory interneurons shape timing, sparsity, and gain 27, 33, 1. This architecture performs an enormous expansion of input dimensionality. In humans, the cerebellar cortex contains tens of billions of granule cells, more than half of all neurons in the brain, and each Purkinje cell receives on the order of one million parallel-fiber synapses 1, 29. This expansion gives the cerebellum a kernel-like representational geometry: mossy-fiber inputs are projected into a huge, temporally structured granule-cell basis, from which Purkinje cells can learn precisely timed predictions and corrections 34, 25, 26. Diedrichsen’s 2026 review gives the useful modern formulation: the cerebellum looks like a high-capacity learning engine that provides precisely timed predictive signals learned from very high-dimensional input 1.

The feedforward character of this architecture is central. Neocortex is massively recurrent and well suited for persistent latent-state inference, attractor dynamics, sequence modeling, and hierarchical generative modeling. The basal ganglia are looped, inhibitory, and disinhibitory, well suited for gating, policy selection, reinforcement, and vigor control. The cerebellar cortex, by contrast, is largely a fast feedforward expansion-and-readout system: inputs enter through mossy and climbing fibers, are transformed through granule, parallel-fiber, Purkinje, and nuclear stages, and leave through deep nuclei and vestibular nuclei 29, 4. Its internal recurrence appears limited compared with neocortex; its computational power comes less from self-sustaining internal dynamics and more from the breadth of its basis expansion, the precision of its timing mechanisms, and the strength of its teaching signals 27, 33. This makes the cerebellum an ideal substrate for learning mappings that must be fast, stable, and automatically deployed once learned.

The cerebellum is also modular. Rather than one homogeneous controller, it is organized into many partially independent modules or microcomplexes, each defined by a linked set of mossy-fiber inputs, climbing-fiber inputs from inferior olive, Purkinje-cell microzones, and nuclear output neurons 35, 36. The modules share a common circuit motif but differ in what they receive and where they project. A vestibulo-ocular module can learn eye-movement calibration; a spinocerebellar module can predict limb dynamics; a cerebro-cerebellar association module can help calibrate prefrontal, language, or social-cognitive dynamics. This repeated-module design makes a single-algorithm account attractive: one conserved circuit, one local computation re-parameterized per territory. But the inference from uniform anatomy to uniform computation is contested. Diedrichsen and Ivry pose a universal transform (one algorithm everywhere) against multiple functionality (the same circuit running distinct computations, each needing its own algorithmic account), and use cerebellar functional heterogeneity as evidence against the former 37. It is therefore best to treat predictive calibration as an organizing hypothesis, not an established universal transform.

Overall, the cerebellum is introduced here as the brain’s high-capacity predictive calibrator: a modular, relatively feedforward, error-trained system that learns how ongoing states will unfold and how selected actions should be corrected before delayed feedback can arrive. It is “motor” in its historical and most clinically obvious role, but not in its full computational scope. Its deeper function is to keep behavior continuous across time: to make action, perception, thought, affect, and social interaction unfold with the right timing, gain, and anticipatory structure 2, 38, 1. The next subsections treat cerebellar learning in the same loss->error->plasticity->learning-in-action sequence used for cortex and basal ganglia, but with a different central question: what losses does a predictive calibration system minimize, what teaching signals carry those errors, and how does its distinctive circuit architecture convert them into precisely timed internal models?
